Write a complete fantasy novel of about 20,000 words.

Premise:
A supposedly benevolent institution—known to outsiders as the Mercy Academy—accepts one hundred girls each year into its care, yet after ten years only three ever walk back out; among those who entered by choice is Rue, who sold herself into the Academy as a young woman and spends the rest of her life there, until in her old age a war finally arrives at the Academy's gates and forces the past and the place to reckon with one another.

Central conflict:
Rue must confront the long-term consequences of having bound herself to an institution that keeps almost everyone it takes, as an encroaching war threatens the Academy and forces hidden realities into the open.

Characters:
- Rue — the woman who willingly entered the Mercy Academy by selling herself.
- The Hundred — the yearly cohort of girls purchased or acquired by the Academy (collective).
- The Three — the rare survivors who leave the Academy after ten years (collective).
- Headmistress — the senior administrator and public face of the Academy.
- War Envoy — a representative or manifestation of the war that reaches the Academy in Rue's old age.

The finished novel must contain all of the following:
- The story must feature an institution that annually acquires one hundred girls.
- It must establish that after a ten-year period, only three individuals ever leave the institution.
- The protagonist, Rue, must have entered the institution by selling herself into it.
- A war must arrive at the institution during Rue's later years, affecting her and the Academy.

Write the novel itself — no outline, no commentary, no notes to the reader.

Propose about 17 scenes of roughly 1176 words each. Give every character, location and significant object a stable id now — later scenes can only refer to entities that exist. State the world rules the story must not break. Then call submit_plan.

entities.sketch: Rue — A woman who sold herself into the Mercy Academy as a young woman. Quiet, practical, and watchful, she spends decades inside the Academy and grows into its reluctant conscience.
The Hundred — The Academy's annual cohort: one hundred girls acquired each year and folded into its programs. They are both a number and a shifting constellation of friendships, rivalries and losses.
The Three — The near-mythic set of alumni who, historically, have left the Academy after ten years. They are spoken of like miracles and warnings at once.

Headmistress — The senior administrator and public face of the Mercy Academy. Polished, diplomatic and possessed of practical ruthlessness; she embodies the Academy's benevolent rhetoric and its hard edges.
War Envoy — A representative of the approaching war: formal, implacable and strange. He/they arrive with offers and threats that make the Academy's hidden arrangements surface.
Mercy Academy — A high, walled institution on an island quartered between harbor, rose gardens and glasshouses. It calls itself sanctuary and school; its walls hold more than classrooms.
Great Hall — The Academy's ceremonial heart: where the Hundred are received, where names are read into the folio and where the Headmistress meets visitors.
Ink Room — A locked room below the library where the Academy's ledgers and the binding inks are kept. Staffed by a small, generational guild of scribes.
Contract — The ledger contract each recruit signs. On its face it promises education and safety in return for ten years; its margins hold clauses not printed for patrons.
Folio — The Academy's ceremonial book that bears the names of every girl who entered and every name that was allowed to leave. It is heavy, stained and glossed with old inks.
Amber Bell — A small bell rung whenever a cohort is closed or when a departure is recorded in the folio. Its sound is both celebration and seal.
Binding Seal — A wax-and-ink sigil used in finalizing contracts; it carries a sorcerous tether that makes some of the Academy's claims enforceable.
Aya — A bright, quick-witted recruit in Rue's first cohort at the Academy; she becomes Rue's close friend and an emotional anchor early in Rue's life there.
Loren — An older instructor who teaches craft and discipline to the Hundred. Stern but humane, he mentors Rue across decades and becomes one of the few inside the walls whom she trusts.
Elaine — One of the named individuals counted among the Three. She left the Academy years ago and lives beyond the city; she carries a scar the Academy never explains.
Maris — Another of the Three. She left under different circumstances and is used by the Academy as an example of success.
Sal — The third of the Three, quieter and more evasive; rumours say she left with secrets the Academy does not want repeated.
Archive Key — A small iron key, stamped with the Academy's crest, used to open the deepest cabinets in the Ink Room and the library's sealed stacks.

arguments.logline: Rue, who sold herself into the Mercy Academy, spends a lifetime inside the institution that annually accepts one hundred girls but returns almost none; when war reaches the Academy's gates in her old age, buried bargains and the Academy's true price are forced into daylight, and Rue must reckon with what she once bargained away.

scenes.intent: Open the novel on the transaction: Rue's decision to sell herself and sign the Contract. Establish the Mercy Academy's public face, the rule that it takes one hundred girls each year, and the notorious statistic that after ten years only three ever walk back out. Introduce the Contract, the Folio and the Headmistress as symbols.

Show the Hundred's arrival: induction ritual in the Great Hall and first night. Rue meets Aya and senses the work the Academy does—education braided with discipline. The Folio is read; the Amber Bell is rung. The scene quietly suggests that the Academy gives girls skills but also takes something else.

Depict the early years of training: classrooms, gardens, the Ink Room glimpsed. Introduce the Ink Room as a strange repository and the Binding Seal in passing. Rue learns craft and learns to measure the Academy's quiet demands. The Three are invoked as stories told to keep girls in line.

Close-up on Rue's interior life and her bond with Aya. Show why Rue sold herself—family debt, a promise—and what she hoped the Academy would be. Record small kindnesses and micro-violences, establishing the Academy's ambiguous benevolence.

A meeting with the Headmistress in which the Academy's public rhetoric—rescue, education, charity—is made explicit. The Headmistress is persuasive about duty and result; her language glosses the Contract's margins. Rue senses double speech and leaves with more questions.

A year marker: the Academy's patron ceremony and the closing of the cohort ledger for that year. The number of new entrants is reiterated and the myth of the Three is placed alongside official praise. Rue begins to take on apprentices and becomes part of the institution's machinery.

Tension builds: Rue discovers a discrepancy in the Folio and asks questions; senior staff are evasive. The idea that the Academy does not merely shelter but binds people becomes firmer. The Ten-Year period is framed as a crucible whose exits are historically vanishingly rare.

Rue finds a half-hidden clause in an old Contract that references a binding ritual and a tether. The Binding Seal's mechanics are hinted at—what it costs and how it ties people to the Academy's ledger. Rue's moral fog thickens; she remembers her younger self signing willingly.

Montage across decades: Rue ages, becomes an instructor and anchor. The narrative shows the Hundred as a cycle, friendships forming and dissolving, the three alumni used in different ways by the Academy (praise, warning, commodity). Time passes and the institution's scale becomes clear.

First sign of the external war: a War Envoy arrives at the harbor to speak with the Headmistress. The envoy's language is formal but unmoving; he carries news that the conflict is swelling toward the island. The Academy's insulated life is threatened for the first time in Rue's memory.

Envoy and Headmistress bartering: the Academy negotiates neutrality, offers shelter, and argues its civic usefulness. The envoy hints at demands—bonds, levies or recruits—that unsettle the Headmistress. Rue listens and realises the war will not be kept at bay by rhetoric.

One of the Three returns to the Academy with a story that complicates the Headmistress's narrative: Elaine (or Maris or Sal) brings news from the outside that hints at what the Academy extracts for itself, and why so few leave. Their presence fractures the ritual certainties inside the walls.

The Academy divides. Some staff and students insist on bargaining with the Envoy; others want to reinforce the gates or to free themselves. Rue is pulled between defending a place that preserved much of her life and acknowledging what it cost others. The Headmistress makes a choice that forces conflict.

The siege begins. The war's instruments strike the island's approaches; the Academy's defenses—both mundane and those tied to the Binding Seal and Folio—are activated. The cost of the Academy's bargains is made physical; the Hundred pay in fear, history and sacrifice.

The Folio reveals what the Binding Seal actually took: a ledgering of lives and a mechanism that prevented departure for most. The Three's exit had costs: names exchanged, bargains fulfilled elsewhere. The Academy's myth of rescue is stripped to its ledgered reality; Rue must confront the life she chose to sell.

Rue's reckoning and the final choice: negotiate with the War Envoy, use the Binding Seal, or break the Folio's hold. Rue executes a plan born of experience and sacrifice that alters who may leave. The scene resolves the personal arc—Rue owning the consequence of her sale—and sets the Academy's new trajectory.

Aftermath: show the new ledger of the Academy and its consequences for the survivors, Rue's last days and how the island changes. The ending is neither wholly punitive nor wholly redemptive; it asks what we owe ourselves and others when we sign contracts in desperation.

world_rules: The Academy accepts exactly one hundred girls into a cohort each year; this number is public and rigid in the story's social systems.

Historically, after a ten-year period inside the Academy, only three individuals have left and their departures are recorded in the Folio (this historical fact is established early and treated as canon unless explicitly changed by a scena-level event with provenance).
Contracts the recruits sign are legally and magically binding when sealed with the Binding Seal; the Seal enacts the Academy's claims but requires the Academy's own rituals to be maintained.

Magic has a cost: any enchantment that binds a person's freedom draws from the same ledger as the Folio and must be accounted for in the Academy's records; bargains cannot be silently created or negated without record.
The War Envoy represents external political/military forces; he may demand terms, levy burdens, or threaten force, but he cannot invent or erase Academy records — only expose and exploit them.

The Folio truthfully records entries and departures; it can be read and misread, hidden, or weaponised, but altering historical entries is itself an action with consequences and must be shown on-page when it happens.
The Headmistress is powerful within the Academy but not omnipotent; she must work within political constraints, her staff and the Academy's rituals.
No deus ex machina: solutions to the Academy's bindings must arise from revealed rules and the characters' established resources and relationships, not from unexplained new powers.

The first time Rue saw the Mercy Academy close up, it was tighter than the pictures had suggested: a band of pale wall against the sky, glasshouses like ribs, and a low harbor crowded with lighters that smelled of salt and coal. She came in winter, with her thin cloak buttoned against wind that knew the island's name and spat it out. The Great Hall stood with its doors open like a mouth of hospitality; under the portico the Headmistress waited in a collar that was more law than ornament. She smiled as if she had shown that smile before and found it useful.

“One hundred this year,” the Headmistress said when the ledger was handed over. “One hundred and none wasted.”

They read the names aloud. The Folio lay on a dais, its binding dark with old oils and the hands of scribes; the voice that read the names had the patient cadence of someone who had watched girls become a rhythm. Amber light stained the pages where ink had soaked into leather. An Amber Bell hung by a silver hook; when it rang the sound filled the Hall and closed the bargain, a neat note of sound that said both welcome and sealing. Rue had come with a purse that held the price of a clause and a will that weighed less than her own need. She came because her mother was ill and her brothers' debts were songs that would not stop, and because there was a phrase on the small handbill one of the lighters had given her that said Mercy Academy: refuge, education, honourable placement. The phrase had fit a long way into the hollow where hope sat.

She signed the Contract in a clean hand that trembled at the end. It promised education, shelter, apprenticeship, the learning of trades and the promise of a place to stand after ten years. The margins, as the Academy’s lawyer later explained, were for technicalities. “We cannot take everyone,” he said, sliding a pamphlet across the table. The pamphlet set the year’s cohort at exactly one hundred girls, explained the Academy’s charitable charter, and listed the civic patrons who kept the island alive. The Headmistress nodded; her voice made the island’s mercies sound like civic virtue.

“You will be safe. You will learn. In ten years—” she looked at Rue the way one inspects a document, “—three have returned. Three is our record, and they speak for what we have been able to do.”

Rue put her thumb to the wax that the scribe pressed into the Contract. The Binding Seal smelt of beeswax and a bitter iron tang, a careful scent like a first prayer. She heard the faint click of ink against vellum and something like a coil unbent in the basement of the Academy, and for a second she saw the ledger it would write on, not yet open to her name. She paid the purse that the procurer asked for, the money taken from the little savings she had scraped, and the sea took the last of her ordinary life and boiled it down.

After the bell she walked the gardens in a kind of disbelief. The Academy was, insofar as the city believed anything, a place where girls were taught to stitch and to read books, to prune roses and to handle good clients at the patron tables. Children left with needles and numbers, with an ability to stand in the world and be usefully womaned. The Headmistress’s speeches said “rescue” and “empowerment” and the city paper printed them obediently. But there were things they said as if they were only proper to be heard in a quiet room: that the Folio recorded both admission and leaving, and that names put in it were not a promise but a ledger—legal things of paper given force by the Seal.

On the first night the Hundred were assigned to rooms that smelled of lavender and damp stone. Rue shared a low bed with Aya, a girl thinner than her who smiled at Rue until the smile became familiar and then necessary. Aya talked too fast and laughed at the wrong times and knew how to hide a bread crust wrapped in a rag in the hems of her skirt. “I came because my father told me married would be worse,” she said, leaning toward Rue as if they were conspiring. They lay awake counting their bargains. The Amber Bell tolled once again, a private echo in the dormitory that belonged to the older girls.

There were lessons every day: the right way to hold a needle, the right word to say when a patron asked how your mother was, the scriptures the Academy thought proper even if they were more civic than holy. There were also tasks that no brochure mentioned—ledgers to fill, small clerical pains that sharpened fingers and blurred clocks. In the Ink Room Rue saw the Folio at close range: its pages turned with ceremonious care, the names already written in columns that drew the life the girls now offered into a tidy graph. “We keep things,” an old scribe said without looking up. “We keep them clean.”

Months became years. Rue learned to mend a winter coat so the stitches did not show; she learned to make a stew that could be plated in a patron’s hall; she learned to read the Folio with a kind of practitioner’s eye. The Binding Seal was explained by rote: it anchored a contract to the Academy and, through the Seal’s ritual, bound an obligation to the ledger. It was not, the instructors insisted, a prison. “Only three have left,” Loren, Rue’s teacher in craft and discipline, reminded the girls. He was not married to the Academy with ribboned speeches; he taught with a dry touch and an honest face. “Three is not nothing. Three is—” he paused, and his look made it clear he accepted the number as both miracle and indictment.

Rue kept waiting for the day when the promise of ten years became the promise of a life outside the walls. She’d told herself she would leave the Academy with skills as fine and useful as a new dress. She would send money home, help her mother; she would set small lives right. She had not considered that the ten years might be a crucible designed to change people until they did not want out, or that the contract’s fine print could carry an aftertaste of iron.

In the Ink Room, late one evening, Rue found a ledger with pages discoloured by centuries of ink. It was catalogued not for public view. The Archive Key was small and iron-worn and when she took it to the cabinet a scribe looked at her with something like pity. “You don’t need to be here,” he said. He closed the door behind her and she saw, on a shelf under dust, a stack of old Contracts. One’s ink had faltered at the margin, and a note in a handwriting that might have belonged to an earlier Headmistress mentioned “tethering.”

The clause read like a promise made to itself: that care might sometimes require impermanent sacrifices, that the Academy’s work asked not only for learning but for a period of binding, in order that the ledger could be balanced. It spoke of names given in exchange—that the Folio recorded departures only when an exchange of names or obligations was accomplished. It was written in the dry voice of bookkeeping and the furtive tone of a person making a calculation in the night. Rue felt the cold of something under her ribs: when she had signed, she had known she was paying with coin. She had not thought she might have paid with a tether she could not see.

Years folded. Aya married the Academy in its particular way—she took a post in the herbarium and never left on the edge of ten years; she told Rue later, in a voice that broke, that she had seen the city from a window once and had turned back to her work, and though she did not say the word, Rue heard “bound” in the way she said “work.” Loren grew older and kept teaching. The Academy became Rue's life by slow accretion. She taught the new Hundred—girls who arrived with the same emptiness and the same clutch of papers at their throats. Sometimes, at dusk, she would open the Folio and run her finger down the list of names, looking for the ones who had left. The Three were three thin paragraphs in the Academy’s public history: Elaine, Maris, Sal. Each had left in a different season, each with a story the Headmistress liked to tell as moral. Rue memorized their names as one remembers the names of saints or storms.

Decades changed Rue’s hands from soft to callused. Her hair stayed dark long enough for the Academy to call her “mature” and “steady.” She rose to be an instructor, and with position came complicity. She told girls sternly to be grateful; she told girls to practice their stitches until they did not hurt. She told herself she had learned to give value for value. When she taught the ritual of sealing a Contract—how to place your signature, how to touch wax, how to stand while the Bind was closed—she felt, under her skin, the old price she had paid. The Headmistress continued to smile as if the smile was a civic effectuality. Under the skins of the younger girls, she saw the same hunger she had carried as a child.

The first news of the war came in the form of a dispatch boat, and with it a man whose cloak had the smell of iron-smoke and the tiredness of border roads. The War Envoy stepped onto the Academy’s wharf as if he expected to be refused and then was surprised he was not. He sat in the Great Hall and spoke without malice and without needless brittleness. “We are at the gates,” he said. “We do not ask for the Academy to choose sides, only for it to be useful.” His tone suggested that usefulness might take the form of bounty, of shelter, of recruits. The Headmistress replied with the phrasing the Academy had grown expert in: neutrality, humanitarian shelter, safe harbor. She offered the Academy’s storerooms and its kitchens. She parried the Envoy’s look with assurance that the Academy could be a place of civic service.

Rue listened from the back. The Academy’s languages—rescue, charity, education—sounded suddenly thin. They were good words, but the world outside had other words. The Envoy’s calmness was not a kindness; it was a ledger. He did not threaten loudly. He did not have to. He had the force of courts behind him and the mathematics of siegecraft. “We will honor the Folio,” he said. “We will honor deeds. We will not see your sanctuary burn unnecessarily.”

After the Envoy left the gardens smelled of a different kind of iron. Some students wanted to bargain with him—parade the Academy’s virtue and ask for charted protection under the war’s banners. Others wanted to refuse any external hand. The Headmistress gathered the older instructors in the Great Hall and turned her face, which was not unkind, toward the problem of survival. Her mind worked in careful arithmetic. She knew the city’s magistrates, the cost of bread beneath siege, and the way to make an envoy think your place was a civic resource instead of a familiar to be picked clean.

Then someone the Academy had not expected stepped across the threshold: one of the Three returned. Elaine’s hair had grown white at the temples and she walked with a scar across her throat like a geography of memory. She came back not as the Headmistress’s emboldened success story but as a bearer of a different report: the city beyond the Academy was hungry, its promises dry as bone, and the Academy was not always a mercy so much as a mechanism for shifting burdens.

“I left,” Elaine said at the gathering, “and I saw trade routes burned and promises eaten. I saw what the Academy sent in exchange for departures.” Her voice was steady; she named no names, but the way she let the sentence hang made the Headmistress’s eyes shadow. “There are places where a name being released requires a debt taken. There are places that ask for blood in exchange for passage.”

The Great Hall went cold as if someone had opened a door to a winter room. Rue felt the old ledger move in the air, a draft from an unopened cabinet. The Headmistress’s face, previously a wall of hospitality, showed flash circuits of resolve. She did not deny that the Folio held exchanges; she reinterpreted them as necessary, as painful and clean. “Three have returned,” she said. “Three have returned because the Academy can make difficult trades.”

The war taught the Academy that nowhere is an island. When the first barges were set on fire and the harbor’s patrols counted losses, the island’s wall felt thinner. The Envoy’s language sharpened: the war could come close enough to make the Academy’s neutrality a paper shield. He asked, in a way that resembled bookkeeping, for the Academy’s ledgered goods—stores, sanctuaries, perhaps, recruits for the front. The Headmistress, pragmatic and fatalistic, made a choice that she thought would keep the Academy alive. She offered certain stores and a handful of names—names not yet recorded as departures, names she thought the city could spare in defense—if the Envoy would promise restraint and honor.

Rue could not reconcile the trade: she had taught that the Academy kept girls safe, that the Bind was a temple of careful law. But she also knew the Folio’s ledgering: names were not abstract, they were exchangeable. She had seen those exchanges in the Archives, written in cramped ink when the city demanded a sacrifice here and the Academy had accounted for it there. The Binding Seal was not merely ink and wax; it was a practice of reciprocity with teeth.

When the first mortar thundered and the island’s harbors filled with smoke, the Academy’s defenses were tested. The Seal’s rituals were performed in the Ink Room with the kind of mechanical reverence apprenticeship had taught for decades. They had men in the tower, with ladders and rope and nets and oil. The Amber Bell was rung to mark each closure and each departure—its clang a sound of braiding and of finality. The Hundred did what they had been trained to do: they sheltered, they stitched, they fed, but under the shelter lay a history of people traded and names switched. The war pulled those names forward like a hand uncoiling.

When the Folio was opened to the center of the Ink Room, it did not lie. It listed names and dates and the thin, bureaucratic language of exits. But when Rue looked closer—when she pried with the Archive Key and the slow patience of someone who had read the ledger for years—the Folio yielded notes in margins, crossed entries, and a faint, almost-erasured ledger of obligations. The Binding Seal—wax and iron and carefully mixed tincture—had a price. It tethered in a way that made leaving costly. It required duties to be paid. The Three had each left because of different exchanges; Elaine had spoken of blood debts, Maris had left by a patron's favour that could not be replicated, and Sal—who rarely returned—had left because she bore confidences the Academy could barter.

The war made those debts material. The Envoy wanted names in a way the city’s magistrates did not; he wanted to shape the population with the same lightness the Academy had used in its earlier accounting. Rue found herself at the center in a way she had not expected. She had been inside long enough to stand in the place between memory and procurement. She had a ledger’s memory and a teacher’s hands. If the Academy could write lines in ink, she could read their consequences. If the Folio held the power to bind, the Seal’s mechanics were on the page: it took kinds of obligations and returned kinds of passage. There was no miracle described, only practice.

There are no easy endings in libraries where the books were written by committees and by desperate hands. Rue understood, finally, that the life she had chosen—the life she had bought with coin and will—was not a free thing to be carried like a possession; it was a part of the academy’s economy. The war asked her to account. The Headmistress accounted too, and in her accounting she made a choice the younger instructors did not like: she would trade a number of unrecorded claims for passage, and she would tie certain girls to the city’s defense in a way that made them instruments rather than apprentices.

Rue could have accepted the arithmetic. She could have kept her place, taken her wage, and taught the next Hundred how to make practical lives of their bindings. Instead she walked to the Ink Room and asked for the Archive Key. She sat with the Folio and the Seal and the looping, patient ink of the scribe. She read every clause that had been inked, every margin note, every old signature. Then she did something the Headmistress had expected all along by the way she had taught Rue to be precise: she made a ledger of her own.

It was not a miracle. It was a ledger entry. Rue found ways to redraw exchanges by naming obligations aloud, by making tender, evident trades that could be witnessed. She called on the old scribe’s sense of duty, on the apprentices’ loyalty, on Loren's clear sense of fairness. She negotiated with the War Envoy in the language he respected: accounting. She promised—she traded—what the Academy truly had: the method of the Bind itself, recorded honestly, with all its costs. She proposed that if the Envoy and the city took only from the Academy what the Academy could show it had clear, honest obligations to, then fewer names would be taken by stealth and more lives would be preserved with choice.

It was an ugly calculus and it would mean loss. Rue did not imagine a world where every binding was undone. She knew as well as the scribe who had taught her that ledgering can only shift weight, not deny gravity. But in the act of making the Folio honest, she found a way to let some leave because they had properly paid or because an obligation had been transferred in the light of witnesses. The War Envoy was not moved by morality but by arithmetic: he accepted what could be accounted for.

In the years after the smoke cleared, the island did not return to what it had been. The Academy’s ledger was altered. It listed more departures with more honest margins. There were fewer dark notes of "untendered exchange" and more careful paragraphs of account. Rue lived to see the Folio open to names she had helped untether. The Three were no longer a mythic triumvirate but a set of stories with clearer edges; Elaine, who had returned to tell the truth, left again on terms that did not hide their cost. Maris took a patron’s favor with a clear bill of sale. Sal, who left with secrets, left under witness instead of stealth.

Rue’s last days were not dramatic. She taught less and sat by the greenhouses more. Girls passed her with small thanks. She opened the Folio sometimes and thought of the coin she had paid when she was young and cold. She had wrested from the Academy’s accounting not a full forgiveness but a kind of integrity. That was something—an echo rather than a repair. The Amber Bell still rang when the ledger closed a year’s entries, and the sound had lost none of its power. It had shifted, the way a bell’s ring shifts when the metal is tempered differently. Rue had kept her life inside and reshaped what that life had been worth.

When she finally left—if leaving for an old woman can be called such—she did so in the public record as part of an exchange the Academy could stand behind. She walked past the glasshouses and the harbor and did not tremble. She had sold herself when she was young, and in the selling she had been given years that kept her mother alive and that taught Rue the needle and the ledger. She had not been given everything. But in the last calculations she had learned to be precise in trade and human enough to make the trade matter.

Outside, the city smelled differently; bronze work glinted in a sun that had its own mathematics. The war had not been entirely merciful, and the island had paid as any place must. But Rue walked with a record under her arm—the legal, honest kind—and a small satisfaction that the ledger she had once signed with a youthful certainty was now, at last, more true. The Mercy Academy still called itself mercy, and the word still had the sharpened edge of economy. Rue had learned to live in that space: not to accept the Academy’s easiest version of itself, nor to tear it down in a single night, but to force the books into light so that choice, however begrudging, might have room.

In the Folio, later scribes would write Rue’s name carefully. The Amber Bell would ring for her exit. Some would call her a renegade, others a hero. The Headmistress would say, in public, that the Academy had changed for the better. Rue did not expect any single story to be true to every life. She thought of the Hundred, of the girls who came in with pockets light and mouths full of names they trusted: she thought of Aya, who had married the herbarium and who came to Rue in the end with eyes wet and hands that smelled of herbs. She thought of the Three, whose departures had been counted as miracles and warnings. She had been one of the Academy’s young bargains; she had grown older inside it; she had, finally, used the craft the Academy had given her to alter what the Academy had always done.

When the last line of ink dried in the ledger that recorded her departure, a scribe closed the Folio with a sure hand. The Amber Bell was rung, and the sound was not the same as it had been years earlier. It was a bell that had learned the notes of truth and ledgered mercy into something closer to what either word might mean.
